title: Events, conditional probability and Bayes
objectives: Calculate conditional probabilities using the correct conditioning denominator and distinguish independence from disjointness.
Derive a posterior from a complete partition and base rates, while keeping model assumptions and impossible evidence explicit.
Apply events, conditional probability and bayes invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: A probability model has outcomes, events and assigned probabilities. An event is a set of outcomes; A∩B means both events occur, A∪B means at least one, and Aᶜ is the complement.

blocks.md: A probability model has outcomes, events and assigned probabilities. An event is a set of outcomes; A∩B means both events occur, A∪B means at least one, and Aᶜ is the complement. Probabilities are nonnegative, the whole outcome space has probability 1, and disjoint event probabilities add. Counting favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes is valid only when those counted outcomes are equally likely. A list of unique scenarios is not automatically a uniform model.

For P(B)>0, $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$. Conditioning restricts attention to B and renormalizes its mass to 1. The numerator is joint mass in both events; the denominator is B, not all outcomes and not A. It follows that $P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B)$. Generally P(A|B) and P(B|A) differ. This finite-event ratio is undefined at P(B)=0; it must not silently return 0. Conditioning in continuous models on exact values needs a conditional-density framework, not this zero-denominator ratio.

blocks.code:
from fractions import Fraction
# Finite synthetic population: each row is equally likely to be selected.
rows = [("fast", True), ("fast", False), ("slow", True), ("slow", True)]
b = [row for row in rows if row[0] == "slow"]
a_and_b = [row for row in b if row[1]]
print(Fraction(len(a_and_b), len(b)))
print(Fraction(len(a_and_b), len(rows)))
print(Fraction(sum(row[1] for row in rows), len(rows)))
blocks.caption: Expected output: 1, then 1/2, then 3/4. Let A be the Boolean True flag and B be the slow group. Both slow rows have the flag, so P(A|B)=1, while P(A∩B)=1/2 and marginal P(A)=3/4. These are probabilities under the declared uniform synthetic population, not estimates validated for a live feed.

blocks.md: Events A and B are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. If P(B)>0, this is equivalent to P(A|B)=P(A). Disjoint events have no overlap; when both have positive probability, they are NOT independent because their joint probability 0 differs from the positive product. Independence is a model assumption or property to justify, not something proved by the word random or by observing two events on different screens. Conditioning also does not by itself establish causation.

Suppose H and Hᶜ form an exhaustive disjoint partition. Every positive signal belongs either to H∩+ or Hᶜ∩+, so $P(+)=P(+\mid H)P(H)+P(+\mid H^c)P(H^c)$. More generally sum over an EXHAUSTIVE disjoint partition, not merely several mutually exclusive events that omit some outcomes. Bayes follows by substituting that total mass into $P(H\mid +)=P(+\mid H)P(H)/P(+)$. A likelihood P(+|H) is not the posterior P(H|+).

blocks.title: A rare condition can yield many false signals
items: Synthetic assumptions: P(H)=0.01, sensitivity P(+|H)=0.9 and false-positive rate P(+|Hᶜ)=0.05.
Among 10000 equally modeled cases, expect 100 H cases and 9900 non-H cases.
Expected true positives 90; false positives 495; total positives 585.
Posterior P(H|+)=90/585=2/13, about 15.38%, not 90%. These counts explain the model arithmetic, not a promised real-world frequency in one sample.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 2/13, then 18/19, then undefined conditional. Keeping the same signal rates while changing the prior changes the posterior. Fraction inputs preserve this finite rational example exactly; they do not remove uncertainty about whether the model inputs are correct.

blocks.md: A posterior calculation is conditional on the stated prior and signal model. If prevalence, selection, regime or signal calibration changes, the result changes. Repeating correlated signals cannot be treated as independent evidence without a justification. A high posterior is not an execution instruction to trade, diagnose or accuse someone. This lesson supplies probability arithmetic and asks you to identify assumptions, not make consequential real-world decisions from synthetic rates.

Independent transfer: make a small 2-by-2 joint probability table with nonnegative masses summing to 1. Compute both conditional directions and verify the product rule. Include a zero-probability conditioning column and reject its ratio. Then change only the prior in a Bayes model and explain which weighted masses change. Test whether an alleged partition is exhaustive before summing likelihood-weighted priors.

References: [Penn State conditional probability](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/book/export/html/485) and [Bayes theorem](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/book/export/html/495). The general partition here explicitly requires exhaustiveness and positive evidence probability. Numeric signal/population fixtures are synthetic, not empirical claims about trading or medical tests.

blocks.caption: Experiment: simulate empirical event frequencies converging to theoretical odds.

guidedExercise.prompt: Before using a computed conditional probability for a real decision, which assumptions would you inspect?
hints: Does not treat a probability as automatic action authority.
guidedExercise.solution: Check the sampled population, event definitions, conditioning information, base rates, signal calibration, dependence, selection/regime changes and whether the decision costs/action policy are actually specified.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Events, conditional probability and Bayes" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: The ratio is joint mass P(A∩B) divided by P(B), with a positive denominator. (Mass inside B is renormalized.)
Disjoint positive-probability events exclude each other, so knowing one occurred changes the chance of the other to 0. (Independence requires equality of those masses.)
The posterior denominator includes positive mass from both the condition and its complement. (They determine how positive mass splits across the partition.)
realWorldApplication: Used directly across production quantitative research, execution systems, and validation pipelines.
quantFinanceApplication: Applies rigorous engineering contracts to quantitative modeling and live trading infrastructure.
summary: Condition on the stated event, not its reverse.
Bayes combines likelihoods with base rates over an exhaustive partition, and its result remains conditional on the model.

quiz.prompt: For P(B)>0, which denominator defines P(A|B)?
options: P(A), because A is written first
P(B), the event being conditioned on
quiz.explanation: The ratio is joint mass P(A∩B) divided by P(B), with a positive denominator. (Mass inside B is renormalized.)

quiz.prompt: Two disjoint events each have positive probability. Are they independent?
options: Yes, because their names are different
Yes, because no overlap is the definition of independence
No; their joint mass 0 differs from the positive probability product
The question is undefined for every finite sample space
quiz.explanation: Disjoint positive-probability events exclude each other, so knowing one occurred changes the chance of the other to 0. (Independence requires equality of those masses.)

quiz.prompt: A signal has sensitivity 0.9 but the condition is rare. What else is needed to compute P(condition|positive)?
options: The prior and false-positive rate as well
Only sensitivity; reverse conditionals are always equal
Only the prior, because every positive signal is equally informative
Only specificity, without the prior or sensitivity
quiz.explanation: The posterior denominator includes positive mass from both the condition and its complement. (They determine how positive mass splits across the partition.)

quiz.prompt: Why must a partition used for total probability be exhaustive as well as disjoint?
options: Disjoint events automatically cover every outcome
Every likelihood must be numerically identical
It prevents probabilities from ever depending on assumptions
Otherwise the denominator omits unlisted evidence mass
quiz.explanation: Summing only part of the population is not the full evidence probability unless omitted groups contribute no mass under a justified model. (Missing groups can make the calculated posterior wrong.)

quiz.prompt: In the worked 10000-case model, there are 90 true positives and 495 false positives. How many total positives enter the posterior denominator?
quiz.explanation: The disjoint positive groups add: 90+495=585. The posterior is 90/585=2/13, not 90/100.
